extracted.intended_audience: writers, critics, philosophers, and students interested in aesthetics, literary criticism, and the psychology of taste
extracted.subtask_description: Principles for judging and producing works of imagination (taste, the sublime, beauty) focusing on how sensation, imagination, and judgment combine to produce aesthetic effects and emotional responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taste as composite of senses, imagination, and judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: What is called taste is not a simple idea, but is partly made up of a perception of the primary pleasures of sense, of the secondary pleasures of the imagination, and of the conclusions of the reasoning faculty concerning their relations and concerning human passions, manners, and actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Taste requires all these elements; because the senses are the originals of our ideas, and the groundwork of taste is common to all, there is a sufficient foundation for reasoning about aesthetic matters. Evaluations should consider sensory impact, imaginative effect, and reasoned judgment about relations and moral/social aspects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensibility (receptivity) as prerequisite to good taste
rubrics_metrics.description: A rectitude of judgment in the arts (good taste) largely depends upon sensibility: if the mind has no bent to the pleasures of the imagination, it will never apply itself sufficiently to works of that species to acquire competent knowledge in them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Creators and critics must account for whether an audience has the sensibility to perceive subtle, refined effects; lack of sensibility (blunt feelings, cold temperament, coarse passions) makes subtle works ineffective for some readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judgment: education, attention, and exercise
rubrics_metrics.description: A defect of judgment (wrong taste) commonly arises from want of proper and well-directed exercise; judgment is improved by extending knowledge, steady attention to objects, and frequent exercise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good critical judgments are the product of training and reflection: avoid rash, prejudiced, or hasty conclusions; cultivated readers 'read with ease and with celerity' but this readiness is the result of practice, not a separate instinctive faculty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causes of wrong taste (errors to avoid)
rubrics_metrics.description: Wrong taste stems from natural weakness of understanding or more commonly ignorance, inattention, prejudice, rashness, levity, obstinacy and other passions that pervert the judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or producing work, beware of these vices: they distort judgment. Critics should be aware of personal biases and temperamental distortions (over-sanguine affectation, excessive passions) that can make poor pieces appear pleasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: NOVELTY
rubrics_metrics.description: Curiosity is the desire or pleasure we take in novelty; 'some degree of novelty must be one of the materials in every instrument which works upon the mind.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Works must include some novelty to attract attention; novelty alone is superficial (curiosity is fleeting), so it must be combined with other powers and passions to sustain interest and produce lasting effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: PAIN AND PLEASURE
rubrics_metrics.description: To move the passions of mature audiences, objects must, besides novelty, be capable of exciting pain or pleasure from other causes; pain and pleasure are simple ideas of a positive nature, distinct from mere relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective imaginative works should register clear sensations of pleasure or pain (not merely by contrast). Critics should distinguish positive pleasure/pain from mere relational effects when assessing emotional impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difference between removal of pain and positive pleasure (DELIGHT)
rubrics_metrics.description: The diminution or ceasing of pain is not the same as positive pleasure; the author uses 'delight' to name the species of relative pleasure that accompanies the removal of pain or danger.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Representations that give relief from danger (escape, release) create a distinct pleasurable effect—'delight'—which differs in quality from positive pleasure. Writers can exploit this distinction (e.g., near-miss, escape scenes) to produce complex responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: JOY AND GRIEF (responses to loss/cessation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cessation of pleasure affects the mind three ways—indifference (simply ceases), disappointment (abruptly broken off), grief (irretrievable loss). Grief often contains pleasure ('pleasing woe') because it keeps the pleasurable object vividly in mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portrayals of grief can be powerfully affecting because they re-present pleasures; grief may be represented as quasi-enjoyable melancholy. Critics should note how works handle absence and loss (whether they create indifference, disappointment, or sustained grief).

rubrics_metrics.name: Passions linked to self-preservation (source of the sublime)
rubrics_metrics.description: Passions concerning self-preservation turn mostly on pain or danger; ideas of pain, sickness, and death fill the mind with horror. These passions are the most powerful and form the basis of the sublime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To access the sublime, works should evoke ideas of pain, danger, or death—powerfully affecting themes tied to survival instincts. But when immediate danger overwhelms, the effect is merely terrible rather than delightful; distance/modification is important.

rubrics_metrics.name: OF THE SUBLIME
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever is fitted in any sort to excite the ideas of pain and danger—terrible objects or analogues of terror—is a source of the sublime, producing the strongest emotion the mind can feel; at certain distances and with certain modifications terror may be delightful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers seeking the sublime should present terror/ danger at a psychological or aesthetic distance or with modifications that allow spectators to feel awe and delight rather than sheer horror. Recognize that death often intensifies the sublime.

rubrics_metrics.name: OF BEAUTY
rubrics_metrics.description: Beauty is a social quality connected with the passions of generation: it inspires tenderness and affection, inclines us to approach and enter relation with its object; beauty functions to fix choice by sensible qualities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beauty in representation should include sensible qualities that produce social/affective responses (tenderness, attachment). For character or erotic depiction, emphasize attributes that produce social attraction and preference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observance of manners, time, place, decency, and congruity
rubrics_metrics.description: Skill in manners and in the observances of time and place and of decency in general is the basis of what is called taste; these are to be learned from philosophy and the world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good works and criticism pay close attention to decorum, congruity, and appropriateness to genre/context. Violations of time/place/decency often indicate poor taste; training in ethics and social knowledge improves judgment here.

rubrics_metrics.name: Society versus solitude (social passions and their pleasures/pains)
rubrics_metrics.description: Society, merely as society, gives no positive pleasure in itself, but absolute and perpetual solitude is a great positive pain; particular social enjoyments give strong sensations of pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Representations involving social contexts should balance the pains of solitude and the pleasures of company; understanding the predominance of pain in the idea of society can inform scenes of isolation or communal delight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sympathy, imitation, and the transmissibility of passion
rubrics_metrics.description: Sympathy allows us to enter into the concerns of others and be moved as they are moved; it is a mechanism by which poetry, painting and other arts transfuse passions and often graft delight onto wretchedness, misery, and death.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Successful imaginative works cultivate sympathy (putting the spectator into another's place) so that feelings are transmitted. Critics and creators should examine how effectively a work induces sympathetic substitution and whether it does so ethically or manipulatively.
